segments.title: The 1801 precedent at Copenhagen
segments.summary: The 1801 attack on Copenhagen and seizure of the Danish fleet provide the immediate precedent for Britain's return six years later.
segments.body: The first Battle of Copenhagen involved Admiral Lord Parker, with Lord Nelson serving as Parker's second in command. The Danish fleet at the capital was destroyed or captured. This outcome establishes the precedent for the 1807 expedition. The second attack follows as a repeat operation against the same fleet and capital only six years later.

evidence.note: The transcript recaps Parker, Nelson, and the capture of the Danish fleet at Copenhagen.

segments.title: Britain returns for the Danish fleet in 1807
segments.summary: Admiral James Gambier returns to Copenhagen in 1807 with Royal Navy and army forces, and the Danish fleet is taken again.
segments.body: Six years after the first attack, the Royal Navy returns under Admiral James Gambier with an army in support. Arthur Wellesley fights Danish troops away from the capital to prevent them from leaving Copenhagen. The operation repeats the earlier pattern, with British forces storming the city and the Royal Navy taking the fleet again. The army supports the naval seizure by holding Danish troops away from the main objective.

evidence.note: The transcript describes Gambier's fleet, accompanying army forces, Wellesley, and the second capture of the Danish fleet.

segments.title: Why Britain repeated the Copenhagen attack
segments.summary: The closing comparison ties both Copenhagen attacks to Britain's effort to keep Danish naval power from joining France.
segments.body: The video closes by placing the 1801 and 1807 attacks side by side: twice within less than a decade, the Royal Navy came to the Danish capital and took its fleet. The stated British rationale is a blunt warning that Denmark should not join France. Control of the Danish fleet connects the two operations. The closing comparison links naval coercion at Copenhagen to British efforts to prevent Danish naval power from joining France.

evidence.note: The transcript compares 1801 and 1807 and states that Denmark should not join the French.
